content: The medication Enfuvirtide, commonly known by the brand name Fuzeon, is used in combination with other antiretroviral drugs to manage HIV infection. It works by reducing the amount of HIV in the body, which helps the immune system function more effectively. However, it is not a cure for HIV. To minimize the risk of spreading HIV to others, patients should continue taking all prescribed HIV medications as directed by their healthcare provider. Additionally, patients should use effective barrier methods, such as latex or polyurethane condoms or dental dams, during sexual activity and avoid sharing personal items like needles, syringes, toothbrushes, or razors that may come into contact with blood or bodily fluids. Enfuvirtide is administered as a subcutaneous injection, typically twice daily, into the upper arm, thigh, or abdomen. It should not be injected into the buttocks or near joints such as the elbow, knee, or groin. Before injecting, the skin at the injection site should be cleaned with rubbing alcohol, and the injection site should be rotated with each dose to reduce the risk of skin injury. Patients should avoid injecting into areas with bumps from previous injections, moles, scars, bruises, tattoos, burns, or the belly button. To reduce bruising, the injection site should not be rubbed after administration. Common side effects include pain, redness, itching, bruising, hardened skin, or bumps at the injection site, which may last up to seven days. Other possible side effects include a runny nose. As the immune system strengthens, patients may experience symptoms of previously undetected infections or an overactive immune response. This reaction, known as immune reconstitution syndrome, can occur shortly after starting HIV treatment or months later. Serious allergic reactions to Enfuvirtide are rare. Patients should inform their healthcare provider if they have any allergies or medical conditions before starting Enfuvirtide. During pregnancy, this medication should only be used when clearly necessary, as it may be part of a treatment plan to reduce the risk of transmitting HIV to the baby. It is unknown if Enfuvirtide passes into breast milk, but breastfeeding is generally not recommended for HIV-infected women to prevent postnatal transmission of the virus. Drug interactions may alter the effectiveness of Enfuvirtide or increase the risk of side effects. Patients should provide their healthcare provider with a complete list of all medications and supplements they are taking. If an overdose occurs, emergency medical attention should be sought immediately. Enfuvirtide should be stored as a dry powder at room temperature before mixing. Once mixed, it should be refrigerated and used within 24 hours. Expired or unused medication should be properly discarded. Regular medical and laboratory tests, such as liver function tests, may be required during treatment to monitor the patient’s response to the medication. Patients should adhere to their prescribed dosing schedule. If a dose is missed, they should contact their healthcare provider for guidance. This medication is no longer expected to be available in the United States after February 28, 2025, as the manufacturer, Genentech, has decided to cease its marketing and distribution due to the availability of newer HIV treatment options.
